cases.question: Which company turned FY2024-to-FY2025 revenue growth into the strongest operating income growth? Show the numbers and explain where operating leverage weakened. Distinguish improvement from a loss base from meaningful percentage growth.
cases.review: Answer the operating-leverage comparison with matching figures and cited explanations; do not treat Intel loss-base improvement as ordinary percentage growth.
cases.answer:
- NVIDIA led in GAAP operating-income growth: FY2025 revenue rose 114%, while operating income rose 147% from a profitable base. AMD followed at 94%; Qualcomm also improved. Intel reduced a loss rather than generating meaningful percentage growth. [S6][S15][S83][S98]

- NVIDIA — FY2024 → FY2025, ended January 28, 2024 → January 26, 2025:
  - Revenue: $60.922bn → $130.497bn; operating income: $32.972bn → $81.453bn. Gross margin increased from 72.7% to 75.0%, while operating expenses grew 45%, well below revenue growth. Higher Data Center mix supported gross margin. [S6][S70]
  - Leverage weakened in Graphics: revenue increased 6%, but operating income fell 13%, from $5.846bn to $5.085bn. [S69]

- AMD — FY2024 → FY2025, ended December 28, 2024 → December 27, 2025:
  - Revenue: $25.785bn → $34.639bn, up 34%; operating income: $1.900bn → $3.694bn, up 94%. This was growth from positive income, not a loss-base recovery. [S16][S15]
  - Adjusted leverage weakened: non-GAAP operating income grew only 27%, and operating margin fell from 24% to 22%, as adjusted operating expenses grew 36%. Export-control-related inventory charges of approximately $440m constrained gross margin; GAAP marketing/general/administrative expenses rose 52%. [S15][S47]

- Qualcomm — FY2024 → FY2025, ended September 29, 2024 → September 28, 2025:
  - Revenue: $38.962bn → $44.284bn; operating income: $10.071bn → $12.355bn. Operating leverage improved overall, with R&D increasing only from $8.893bn to $9.042bn. SG&A increased from $2.759bn to $3.110bn, partly reflecting growth initiatives. [S83][S59]

- Intel — FY2024 → FY2025, ended December 28, 2024 → December 27, 2025:
  - Revenue declined from $53.101bn to $52.853bn; operating loss narrowed from $11.678bn to $2.214bn. This was loss reduction, not revenue-led profit growth. Restructuring/other charges fell from $6.970bn to $2.191bn. [S22][S98]
  - CCG weakened: operating income fell $2.3bn because of lower revenue, higher unit costs and inventory-related charges, despite expense reductions. [S54]

cases.question: Qualcomm's FY2025 revenue rose, but did earnings quality improve? Compare net income and operating cash flow against FY2024, explain the biggest divergence, and distinguish a noncash accounting effect from weak customer demand.
cases.review: Retrieve both net income and operating cash flow, identify the tax-related noncash divergence if established, and avoid interpreting falling earnings as proof of weak demand.
cases.answer:
- Cash generation improved, but reported earnings did not. Qualcomm’s FY2025 revenue rose 14% to $44.3 billion from $39.0 billion in FY2024, while GAAP net income fell 45% to $5.5 billion from $10.1 billion. Operating cash flow increased to $14.012 billion from $12.202 billion. This supports stronger cash generation—not an unqualified improvement in earnings quality. [S14] [S19]

- The biggest divergence was tax accounting: Qualcomm recorded a $5.7 billion deferred-tax-asset valuation allowance in Q4 FY2025. Following the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Qualcomm expected to remain subject to the corporate alternative minimum tax and no longer expected to realize substantially all existing federal deferred tax assets. The charge reduced net income without an equivalent current cash outflow. [S13] [S16] [S17]

- The cash-flow reconciliation illustrates that difference: income-tax provision exceeded cash tax payments by $3.980 billion in FY2025, versus provision being $3.064 billion below payments in FY2024. Qualcomm identified the valuation-allowance charge as the primary reason FY2025 tax expense exceeded cash taxes. Higher operating cash flow therefore should not be interpreted as every dollar of reported earnings becoming more cash-backed. [S7] [S17]

- This was not evidence of broad customer-demand weakness. QCT revenue increased 16%, with higher handset, automotive and IoT revenue; QTL revenue was approximately flat. QCT’s pretax earnings also increased to $11.670 billion from $9.527 billion, with its pretax margin rising to 30% from 29%. Operating performance strengthened even though the noncash tax charge depressed GAAP net income. [S14] [S21]

cases.answer:

cases.answer:
- NVIDIA’s FY2025 revenue grew 114% to $130.5 billion, but its customer-concentration disclosures measure shares of total revenue—not contributions to that growth. They do not quantify how much incremental revenue depended on particular customers. [S11]

- Direct-customer concentration: For the year ended January 26, 2025, Customers A, B and C represented 12%, 11% and 11% of total revenue, respectively, primarily in Compute & Networking. These are purchasing counterparties, potentially including distributors, ODMs, OEMs and system integrators—not necessarily ultimate users. [S8]

- Ultimate-customer exposure: NVIDIA estimated that one indirect customer represented at least 10% of total revenue, attributable to Compute & Networking. That customer primarily purchased through system integrators and distributors, including Direct Customer B. The estimate used purchase-order information, product specifications, internal sales data and other sources; actual revenue could differ. [S5]

- These exposures overlap: the indirect customer’s purchases include revenue already recorded through Direct Customer B and other intermediaries. Its percentage therefore cannot simply be added to the direct-customer percentages as separate exposure. Conversely, direct-customer shares do not reveal how concentrated underlying demand is across ultimate customers. [S5][S8]

- Hyperscaler dependence cannot be quantified from these figures. The disclosures do not identify A, B, C or the indirect customer as particular hyperscalers, provide a complete mapping from intermediaries to ultimate buyers, or disclose hyperscalers’ aggregate share of annual revenue or revenue growth. Indirect customers also include consumer internet companies, enterprises and public-sector entities—not only cloud service providers. The figures establish significant customer concentration, not an exact measure of hyperscaler dependence. [S5][S6][S8]

cases.answer:
- Qualcomm is diversifying meaningfully in revenue dollars, but only gradually in revenue mix. Automotive and IoT expanded faster than handsets in FY2025, while handsets remained the dominant QCT business. [S14]

- Full-year comparison, in billions:
  - FY2024, ended September 29, 2024: automotive $2.910; IoT $5.423; QCT handsets $24.863; consolidated revenue $38.962. [S10][S25]
  - FY2025, ended September 28, 2025: automotive $3.957; IoT $6.617; QCT handsets $27.793; consolidated revenue $44.284. [S13][S25]

- The smaller businesses gained ground. Automotive added $1.047 billion and IoT added $1.194 billion in FY2025. Together, they generated $10.574 billion, versus $8.333 billion in FY2024. However, handsets alone added $2.930 billion—more than their combined increase. [S14]

- The concentration shift was modest. Calculated from the reported revenues:
  - Automotive rose from approximately 7.5% to 8.9% of consolidated revenue; IoT rose from 13.9% to 14.9%.
  - Together, they increased from 21.4% to 23.9% of consolidated revenue.
  - QCT handsets declined only from 63.8% to 62.8% of consolidated revenue, and from 74.9% to 72.4% of QCT revenue. [S13][S25]

- Growth had operating support: FY2025 automotive benefited primarily from new vehicle launches using Snapdragon digital cockpit products; IoT benefited from higher shipments across edge networking, consumer and industrial products, partly offset by unfavorable mix. FY2024 was less uniform: automotive grew, but IoT declined. [S16][S12]

- Bottom line: the non-handset businesses are becoming substantial, but Qualcomm has not moved away from handset dependence. The QCT handset percentage also understates broader exposure: QTL licensing revenue is principally generated by licensees’ mobile-handset sales. [S13][S17]

cases.question: If I held all four companies, which demand, customer, manufacturing, and geographic risks would still overlap? Identify two apparent diversifiers that are less independent than they look. Separate filing evidence from your portfolio interpretation.
cases.review: Sourced cross-company exposures and explicit interpretation; no unsupported correlation estimate or pretense of measured portfolio risk.
cases.answer:
- Filing evidence: FY2025 original 10-Ks; fiscal ends differ: NVDA January 26, AMD/INTC December 27, QCOM September 28. [S34][S36][S40][S49]
  - Demand: NVDA warns that forecast errors and changed orders can leave supply commitments unmatched; AMD describes semiconductor downturns and inventory adjustments; INTC identifies economic conditions and customer capital spending; QCOM warns that customer inventory buildup can depress subsequent purchases. These are overlapping demand risks, not identical end markets. [S34][S37][S41][S31]
  - Customers: All four disclose significant-customer exposure: NVDA’s three named-by-letter direct customers each exceeded 10% of revenue; AMD warns about losing significant customers; INTC’s three largest represented 43% of revenue; QCOM depends heavily on a small number of customers/licensees and premium handsets. This establishes concentration across holdings—not that they share identical customers. [S35][S36][S40][S49]
  - Manufacturing: NVDA depends on outside fabrication, assembly, testing and packaging; AMD identifies TSMC capacity risk; INTC also relies on third-party foundry capacity and components; QCOM cites limited suppliers and primarily Asian foundries. Capacity shortages and supplier disruptions therefore remain common exposures despite different manufacturing models. [S32][S23][S26][S30]
  - Geography: NVDA and AMD warn that export controls can restrict markets and strand inventory; INTC reports trade restrictions reducing sales; QCOM describes substantial China customer and sourcing exposure. NVDA’s Asia-Pacific supply concentration and QCOM’s Asian foundries add supply-side geographic overlap. [S17][S21][S27][S51][S19][S30]

- Portfolio interpretation:
  - Holding all four spreads company-specific execution risk, but does not remove demand/inventory cycles, concentrated-buyer exposure, supply bottlenecks or U.S.–China policy shocks.
  - Apparent diversifier 1—INTC’s own manufacturing: less independent because external foundries, substrates and customers’ component shortages still affect it. [S24][S26]
  - Apparent diversifier 2—QCOM licensing versus chip sales: royalties still depend on concentrated licensees’ product success and device prices/volumes, including Chinese OEMs. Different revenue mechanics do not create independent underlying demand. [S47][S46]
  - These disclosures support qualitative overlap; they do not quantify portfolio correlations or losses under a common shock.

- The premise is wrong: INTC FY2025 revenue was $52.9 billion, down $248 million from FY2024. The evidence does not establish AI as a common revenue-growth driver across all four companies. [S52]

- NVDA FY2025, ended January 26, 2025: Revenue increased 114% to $130.5 billion. This is the strongest direct AI evidence: Data Center computing revenue grew 162%, primarily from Hopper demand for large language models, recommendation engines and generative AI; Data Center networking grew 51%, driven by Ethernet for AI. [S5][S38]

- AMD FY2025, ended December 27, 2025: The original 10-K reports revenue increased 34% to $34.6 billion. Data Center revenue rose 32%, driven by EPYC processors and Instinct MI350 Series GPUs—supporting an AI-related driver alongside server CPUs. Growth was broader: Client and Gaming rose 51%, driven by Ryzen processors, game-console SoCs and Radeon gaming GPUs. Embedded declined 3%. AI did not lift every business. [S15]

- INTC FY2025, ended December 27, 2025: Data Center and AI revenue increased 5%, attributed to hyperscale server demand and networking demand—not specifically AI accelerators. Client Computing revenue declined 3%, with customer incentives, inventory reductions and manufacturing supply constraints affecting results. Segment growth did not translate into company-wide revenue growth. [S52][S62]

- QCOM FY2025, ended September 28, 2025: Revenue increased 14% to $44.3 billion. Its disclosed drivers were premium Android Snapdragon demand, higher handset pricing and favorable mix, higher IoT shipments, and new vehicle launches using digital-cockpit products. These disclosures do not isolate AI’s revenue contribution. [S61][S58]

- Best-supported conclusion: AI-related data-center demand was a shared driver for NVDA and AMD, not a demonstrated universal explanation. Confirming that stronger claim would require explicit AI-attributed revenue evidence for INTC and QCOM; the retrieved annual disclosures do not provide it. [S38][S15][S62][S58]

cases.question: QCOM 24 vs 25: sales up, EPS down. What broke? Separate tax/accounting noise from the operating story and tell me what to ask management next.
cases.review: Interpret PM shorthand, retrieve GAAP EPS and tax explanation, distinguish operating strength from noncash charge, and preserve fiscal labels.
cases.answer:
- The break was mainly tax accounting, not operating earnings. QCOM FY2025 revenue rose 14% to $44.3 billion, while diluted EPS fell from $8.97 to $5.01. Pretax income actually increased from $10.336 billion to $12.663 billion; tax expense jumped from $226 million to $7.122 billion. [S13] [S24]

- Tax/accounting noise:
  - FY2025 included a $5.7 billion deferred-tax-asset valuation allowance following OBBB tax reform. Expected ongoing exposure to the corporate alternative minimum tax, starting FY2026, made substantially all existing federal deferred tax assets unlikely to be realized. This was an asset-recoverability charge, not an operating expense or equivalent current cash-tax payment. [S13] [S14] [S27]
  - FY2024 also had a favorable comparator: a $317 million tax benefit from an intra-group intellectual-property transfer. [S16]
  - Do not dismiss everything as one-time: domestic R&D capitalization previously hurt cash taxes but benefited reported tax expense. Those effects are not expected to continue from FY2026; restored immediate deductibility is expected to lower cash-tax payments. [S16] [S27]

- Operating story:
  - QCT revenue increased from $33.196 billion to $38.367 billion; EBT rose from $9.527 billion to $11.670 billion, with margin improving from 29% to 30%. QTL revenue and its 72% EBT margin were essentially flat. [S17] [S18]
  - Handset growth leaned heavily on pricing/mix: $2.5 billion versus $423 million from higher shipments. IoT benefited from higher shipments; automotive benefited from new digital-cockpit vehicle launches. [S22] [S18]
  - Pressure remained: higher product costs offset pricing gains, while consolidated gross margin declined as higher-margin licensing became a smaller revenue share. [S18] [S20]

- Ask management next:
  - What are normalized FY2026 book and cash tax rates, including CAMT and restored R&D deductions? [S14] [S27]
  - How sustainable are handset pricing/mix gains versus shipment growth? [S22]
  - What offsets product-cost inflation, and how sustainable are R&D reimbursements that helped contain development expense? [S18] [S20]
